t: “We’re the party of common sense”: conflicting appeals to “normal/ity” and “common sense” in the discourse of the Freedom Party of Austria
abs: The political invocation of common sense dates to antiquity and has often been deployed to appeal to the alleged agreements of an epistemic community, rejecting expert knowledge in favor of intuition and “general knowledge” (endoxon), with implicit assumptions about shared values and policies (Boukala Citation2025; Rosenfeld Citation2011; Wodak Citation2024a). Yet these concepts are far from uncontroversial, as they are employed not only by far-right groups but also by progressive grassroots movements and politicians. These distinct meanings of common sense are not merely what Krzyżanowski and Krzyżanowska (Citation2024) term “conceptual flip-siding”, “a process of strategic reversal of notions closely associated with liberal democracy or with its key values of freedom, equality, tolerance and the like, for pronouncedly illiberal gains”, but – as I postulate – a systematic, simultaneous and context-dependent mobilization of diverse meanings (and thus values and ideologies) by far-right and progressive/liberal actors alike. The struggle is thus ultimately over the hegemonic definition of these terms, a struggle which draws on meanings developed over centuries; moreover, both camps claim to propagate the “good” imaginary of a “new normal/ity”.

t: Conceptual flipsiding and reversal of liberal-democratic notions: discursive-political strategies in/and the normalisation of illiberal public imagination
abs: The process of strategically redefining key liberal-democratic and other widely accepted social and political concepts by the far-right and other illiberal actors has recently become a widespread, cross-national phenomenon. Seeing it as integral to both the ongoing mainstreaming of the far right and the ever more pervasive, social-wide normalisation of illiberalism, we define this process as “conceptual flipsiding” and elaborate on it here from a set of interdisciplinary perspectives and in various contexts. We view “conceptual flipsiding” as the key component of illiberal “discursive shifts” in the public sphere that facilitate durable infusion of illiberalism into public discourse by changing the ways of speaking and thinking about key social and political ideas and issues. Exploring both theoretically and empirically the multiple dynamics, trajectories and intricacies of “conceptual flipsiding,” we approach it as a strategic process wherein various public actors contribute to the ongoing illiberal discursive colonisation of liberal-democratic and key social and political concepts. Through our analyses of the discourse-conceptual dynamics surrounding the “conceptual flipsiding”, we observe it as a long-lasting process wherein many of the (once) widely accepted core meanings of key liberal-democratic and other socio-political concepts are not only persistently diluted or weakened but often outright replaced with “new”, illiberal understandings that eventually persist in both public discourse and in public imagination.

t: Who are the “People” and what does “Home” mean? A case of frame transformation and counter-framing of the “People’s Home” in the Sweden Democrat Rhetoric 1989–2022
abs: This article examines how the radical right-wing party, the Sweden Democrats, have reframed and transformed the concept of the People’s Home (folkhemmet) in their political rhetoric from 1989 to 2022. Originally a symbol of Swedish social democracy and egalitarianism, the People’s Home has been repurposed to align with an ethno-nationalist agenda, emphasizing cultural homogeneity and the exclusion of immigrants. Drawing on frame theory, and particularly the concept of frame transformation, the analysis explores how the Sweden Democrats use the concept of the People’s Home to mobilize voters by invoking nostalgia for a perceived “golden age” of safety, consensus, and homogeneity. By mobilizing nostalgia as a political mechanism, the Party undermines political opponents with the aim of attracting mobile voters. The findings show how the Sweden Democrats’ reframing of the People’s Home has contributed to their political mobilization, resonating with voters concerned about immigration and cultural change. The paper reveals the strategic use of nostalgia and ethnic nationalism in radical right-wing parties’ political rhetoric fosters a sense of national identity and unity. The analysis draws on party manifestos, position papers, and election platforms from 1989 to 2022.

t: Science as the enemy: martyrs, prophets, and the delegitimization of medical authority in post-pandemic anti-vaccine discourse
abs: This study examines how anti-vaccine discourse tries to dismantle scientific authority in post-pandemic contexts. Through Critical Discourse Analysis of two contrasting dialogues from Spanish conservative media (one confrontational, one ideologically aligned) we reveal that epistemic delegitimization strategies shift dramatically with audience composition. In confrontational settings, speakers deploy rationalized skepticism and construct 'reasonable layperson' figures; in aligned settings, discourse escalates to moralized conspiracy theories featuring 'epistemic martyrs’ and 'moral prophets.' The analysis, integrating anthropology of knowledge and social semiotics, demonstrates that anti-vaccine rhetoric functions as structured epistemic resistance rather than mere misinformation. By denaturalizing the category of 'denialism,' this work advances discourse studies’ understanding of how alternative knowledge systems challenge institutional authority during crises. The findings carry implications for science communication and public health strategy in digitally mediated environments.

t: Double flipsiding: the liberalisation and illiberalisation of “Security”
abs: This article examines the evolving discourse of security through the lens of “conceptual flipsiding.” Focusing on the notion of security as a “discursive nodal point,” the paper traces two major discursive shifts: the liberalisation of security in the 1980s and 1990s, marked by the rise of human security and the broadening of referent objects beyond the state; and its illiberal reversal that re-nationalises and militarises the discourse, appropriating liberal norms for authoritarian ends. Drawing on discourse theory and securitisation studies, the analysis highlights how core concepts are contested, redefined, and mobilised through strategic discursive practices. I illustrate this “illiberal conceptual flipsiding” focusing on the reappropriation of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) by authoritarian regimes and on gendered securitisation discourses in European right-wing populism. Both of these demonstrate the ambivalence and reversibility of liberal discourses when their internal tensions are left unaddressed. The article argues that flipsiding is not confined to illiberal projects, but is a broader semiotic strategy of hegemonic struggle that exposes the fragility of normative discourses. By linking critical security studies with discourse theory and semiotics, the paper thus contributes to a deeper understanding of how meaning is made, contested, and reversed in the global politics of security.

t: Enacting and rearticulating “accountability”: reactionary watchdogs and the staging of anti-woke culture wars
abs: A commitment to the principle of political accountability is part of the common sense of liberal democratic societies that is particularly important to journalists. It shapes the adversarial posture of a fourth estate narrative where journalists act as watchdog critics “holding power to account” on behalf of the public. This paper examines how the political meaning of accountability talk is “conceptually flipped” in an atmosphere of culture war conflicts where the very idea of critique takes on a reactionary valence. I introduce the concept of the reactionary watchdog – my shorthand for capturing forms of accountability work and (quasi)journalistic practice that normalize a horrific far-right representation of left-wing identities. The notion of reactionary watchdogism blurs any neat distinction between “liberal” and “illiberal” politics and resonates with sedimented institutional logics that are part of the political legacy of neoliberalism. I support the conceptual argument by discussing the case of Christopher Rufo, the US “anti-woke” activist who first came to national prominence by spearheading the attack against critical race theory. I focus on two podcast interviews Rufo did with another exemplary culture war figure, the Canadian psychologist Jordan Peterson.

t: De Rationibus caporali: justification and denial in emerging social representations and ideologies of caporali in migrant agricultural exploitation
abs: This study explores how caporali justify and deny their role in caporalato, a system of migrant labor exploitation deeply embedded in the agricultural sector. While economic and legal analyses have dominated research on caporalato, less attention has been given to the social and discursive mechanisms that sustain it. Using qualitative data from migrant workers, farmers, and agricultural entrepreneurs, the study applies a dual framework of emerging social representations and ideologies to examine how caporali construct narratives that reinforce compliance and discourage resistance. Findings reveal that justification and denial function as central discursive strategies within these representations. Justification frames caporali as necessary mediators rather than exploiters, while denial shifts responsibility away from them, minimizing or obscuring the exploitative nature of caporalato. These strategies shape workers’ perceptions, making resistance less likely. By exposing them, the study argues that efforts to dismantle caporalato must address not only legal and economic dimensions but also the discursive conditions that normalize exploitation.

t: Exclusionary and xenophobic speech in Swedish health care settings: the challenge of “language”
abs: Ability in the local national language is a central object for discourses that de/legitimise immigrants and shape ideas of social reality and social action. In the context of Swedish health care settings, examples of reported speech from patients are offered to show how a presumed migrant’s accent in speaking a national language is conceptually multi-valent in terms of the regulation of legitimacy. Staff who are presumed to be migrants are regularly de-legitimised on the grounds of their speaking style, with foreign accents emphasised as a sign of illegitimacy. Staff who speak without an accent are de-legitimised as speaking Swedish that is too fluent to be compatible with status as an immigrant. The delegitimising of both accented and unaccented language in health care settings indicates the exclusionary and racist nature of language practice, mobilised to delegitimise presumed migrants.

t: Digital gastronationalism: how “white people food” discourse constructs national identity on Douyin
abs: This study investigates the “white people food” (白人饭) meme on Douyin as a manifestation of digital gastronationalism. Through critical discourse analysis of comments on a viral video, the research identifies four strategies transforming everyday food talk into national boundary-work: essentialization of cultural differences; moralization linking cooking to character; somatization framing taste as biological incompatibility; and scientification deploying nutritional and Traditional Chinese Medicine discourse to legitimize hierarchies. These strategies circulate through platform affordances that reward memetic content, fostering a participatory, algorithmically mediated nationalism. Beyond culinary preferences, these debates serve as proxy arenas for negotiating health norms and cultural confidence. The findings demonstrate how ordinary users appropriate and adapt state cultural scripts, making nationalism feel simultaneously inevitable and negotiable within digital environments.

t: “Populism” and the far-right capture of liberal-democratic signifiers
abs: The far right has turned notions such as democracy, equality, freedom and tolerance into rhetorical weapons, not by opposing them in the name of authoritarianism, inequality, unfreedom or intolerance but by using their rhetorical force against liberal and progressive politics and by bending their meaning towards nativist, racist, inegalitarian, anti-feminist, and authoritarian ends. This article asks what role populism plays in this capture of liberal-democratic signifiers. Building on a discourse-theoretical conceptualization of populism as an ideologically flexible political logic, the article constructs an analytical framework for approaching that question. The article first shows how populism is key to the far right’s mobilization of “democracy” against liberal and progressive “elites” but also allows the far right to capture liberal-democratic signifiers such as tolerance and freedom and use them against the “undemocratic elite”. Attention then turns to how liberal-democratic signifiers are articulated with substantive far-right ideology, and what this does to the meaning of those liberal-democratic signifiers. In conclusion, the article reflects on what the far right’s capture of liberal-democratic signifiers tells us about the far right’s relation to liberal-democratic hegemony and about the vulnerability of liberal-democratic signifiers to far-right capture.

t: Multimodal critical discourse analysis of family construction in locally produced high school EFL coursebooks in Türkiye
abs: This study scrutinizes the multimodal representations of “family” in four state-mandated high school English course books published by the Ministry of National Education (MoNE) in Türkiye. Although course books are central instructional tools in English as a foreign language (EFL) classrooms, they also operate as ideological artifacts that circulate selective cultural values. Drawing on the concept of imagined communities and employing multimodal critical discourse analysis, we examine how family is portrayed across MoNE's ELT course books for grades 9–12. The analysis reveals a dominant privileging of Euro-American, nuclear, middle-class, heterosexual, and able-bodied family models aligned with neoliberal ideals of self-sufficiency, positivity, and individual responsibility. Turkish families are largely absent, and the few depictions that appear typically portray older, rural women wearing headscarves; thus sidestepping political debates surrounding the hijab in Türkiye. In contrast, headscarves are more commonly shown on young, modern, non-Turkish women, producing a sanitized representation that obscures the visibility of young, urban, devout Muslim women in contemporary Türkiye. Extended families, when included, are associated with modern leisure activities, positioning family as a vehicle for transmitting neoliberal values rather than as a diverse or contested social institution. Overall, the findings illuminate how these course books erase marginalized identities, local cultures, and sociopolitical struggles while reinforcing an exclusionary “family fairy tale.”

t: Selling China’s story: the multimodal semiotics of positive symbolic communication in national image building through Laowai Wanghong ’s vlogs
abs: This research examines how Laowai Wanghong (foreign internet celebrities) mobilize social media technologies and symbolic communication to “promote China” internationally as part of the propaganda campaign aimed at building China’s international image and strengthening its discourse power. Drawing upon a collection of videos posted on YouTube and using a multimodal critical discourse approach (MCDA), the analysis examines the multimodal resources and discursive techniques employed by “Laowai Wanghong” in creating content as a form of symbolic communication. In our study, we focus on three recurring themes: modern Chinese factories, cultural richness, and a foreigner-friendly environment. Our critical analysis highlights the curated and filtered nature of their portrayals and the implicit alignment with state-driven campaign efforts, reflecting China’s perception of how outsiders view the country; specifically, these topics and content are designed to resonate with international audiences. The study further contributes to a critical understanding of the use of symbolic communication in the representation of China by foreign internet vloggers and to the development of methodological approaches for studying multimodal social media content.

t: Institutional and conceptual flipsiding: illiberal subversion of “democracy”
abs: The paper explores the institutional and conceptual flipsiding of democracy, which belongs to an illiberal and authoritarian repertoire. Firstly, the paper departs from research in the social sciences embracing a wider approach to democracy, including illiberal aspects, which, in effect, dilutes the meaning of democracy. Secondly, the paper explores institutional change that illiberal elites implement with the goal of power hoarding and subversion of democracy. The institutional changes target the scope of democracy with the goal of permanently fixing the power position of the incumbent ruling actors (institutional flipsiding). Moreover, the institutional changes follow an illiberal script to illiberalism which is common to all autocratizing regimes. Thirdly, the paper deals with the conceptual subversion (conceptual flipsiding) targeting the meaning of democracy, as it attempts to dissociate democracies from their liberal fundaments, such as civic and political rights. It concludes that illiberal regimes are prone to masquerading as democracies. They do so by changing both the scope and meaning of democracy, as they want to pass as democracies, both in front of domestic and foreign audiences.

t: Unpacking gamification in CALL: a sociocultural and multimodal analysis of digital game-based language learning
abs: Digital Game-Based Language Learning (DGBLL) has become an increasingly visible strand of Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL), producing a substantial body of research on games’ positive contributions to second language acquisition. However, despite the increasingly sophisticated research design, much DGBLL work continues to follow a familiar experimental template: pre/post tests, observations, and surveys that operationalize game features under a broad “gamification” umbrella . Indeed, this paradigm makes strong claims about effectiveness while leaving the linguistic and semiotic resources in gameplay under-described – what we call the “black box” of gamification. Regarding the discovered issues, applying sociocultural theory and multimodal analysis, we examine how language is deployed in a worldwidely played simulation game Animal Crossing. We analyze how multimodal resources – such as text, icons, 3D character actions, and spatial arrangements – create authentic contexts, scaffold communication, and embed cultural practices. The findings demonstrate how language serves multiple functions in various gameplay and scenarios – as a medium of interaction and a symbolic tool that supports meaning-making, identity construction, and affective engagement. It suggests that CALL research can benefit from closer attention to the linguistic and semiotic textures of gamification, thereby complementing outcome-focused studies with theoretically grounded accounts of how games themselves operates as meaningful learning environments.

t: Reduced moral culpability: discursive practices by perpetrators and accomplices of honor crimes in the Arab world
abs: This study examines how perpetrators and accomplices (P&As) of honor crimes in the Arab world discursively construct moral accountability in televised interviews. The aim is to understand how language is used to justify or legitimize acts of honor-based violence. Using a Discursive Psychological (DP) approach, the study analyzes televised interview transcripts with individuals involved in honor crimes. The analysis focuses on how interviewees use language to construct identities, assign blame, and invoke cultural norms, with attention to discursive features such as script formulations, category entitlements, and stake management. The analysis reveals that P&As often portrayed themselves as ordinary and morally constrained individuals, while casting the victims as bearers of shame or threats to family honor. Script formulations and references to prevailing social expectations were used to depict the crimes as inevitable or necessary. Responsibility was frequently displaced onto the community, cultural traditions, or familial obligations, particularly when direct justification of the act was problematic. These findings show how honor-based violence is normalized and moral accountability is diffused through everyday discourse. By unpacking the discursive strategies that legitimize such violence, the study underscores the importance of disrupting cultural narratives that sustain honor-based violence. This has critical implications for legal, social, and educational interventions aimed at prevention and accountability.

t: Reproductive rights and the recontextualization of abortion: a multimodal analysis of ballot initiatives in the US
abs: The overturning of Roe v. Wade and resulting abortion bans in the United States have led to dire consequences for women. Case in point, in 2024, ballot initiative 434, which proposed an existing 12-week abortion ban to be enshrined in the constitution, passed in Nebraska. This was despite previous polls showing most Nebraskans did not support it. The present paper examines the initiative’s promotional materials to explore which strategies may have contributed to the victory of 434 over 439, and what discourses were drawn on and reproduced during the campaign. Drawing on (feminist, multimodal) critical discourse studies, the author analyzed 22 promotional materials related to ballot initiative 434 using one of them to illustrate patterns in the data. Findings reveal various far-right populist strategies involved in recontextualizing abortion through transformations such as deletions, substitutions, and additions. The author concludes by raising awareness about recent trends in far-right populist discourse and campaign strategies and suggesting strategies for counter discourse.

t: Representations of “Divorced” in Turkish media on psychological health: a multimodal critical discourse analysis
abs: Employing Multimodal Critical Discourse Analysis, this study examines the concept of “divorced” on Turkish psychological health websites to explore the emotional and psychological dimensions of divorce concerning the individuals involved. Grounded in the principles of Critical Discourse Analysis, the study investigates how ideologies and social assumptions are reproduced through both textual and visual modes. The analysis shows that divorce is overwhelmingly depicted as a negative event through metaphors, analogies and overgeneralizations. The assumed emotional and psychological harm to children receives the greatest focus. Gendered stereotypes are evident as women are depicted in both positive and negative ways, while men, with minimal emphasis in amount, are largely portrayed negatively regarding their emotional state and post-divorce fathering behaviors. Ignoring individual differences, the data frequently present divorce as having predictable and uniform consequences. The visual elements also consistently enhance the textual content through the use of body language, gaze, facial expressions, color tones, spatial arrangements, visual metaphors and strategic points of focus. Furthermore, a dominant ideology of heteronormativity, which fortifies traditional gender roles and expectations, is evident throughout the data.

t: “Cleaning up after capitalism”: recentring blue-collar work in the spatial semiotics of waste
abs: Seemingly banal and certainly backstage, washrooms are epitomic sites of wasting/cleaning. Allied with sociolinguistic interest in blue-collar work/places, this paper envisions luxury washrooms in high-end shopping malls as an ideal space for tracing the organisation of waste work and workers. Drawing on a larger discourse-ethnographic study, and grounded in geosemiotic principles, my analysis identifies three spatial-semiotic strategies by which habitual relations with bodily waste are organised: (1) documentary regimes and/as surveillant landscapes; (2) technologies of un/knowing and in/visibility; and (3) micro-landscapes of cleaning labour and makeshift life. Each of these strategies is documented and illustrated by means of photographic evidence. In the spirit of complicating centre-periphery power dynamics, I centre elite washrooms as sites of neoliberal work inequality, ultimately surfacing the marginalised experiences of blue-collar work communities as they are lived, interpreted, and contested anew.

t: Mobilising through fear: the semiosis of Kremlin strategic conspiracy narratives
abs: This article analyses the strategic use of emotionally charged history narratives in Russian state discourse, focusing on the framing of the Soviet Union’s collapse as a “geopolitical catastrophe” and the glorification of the Second World War victory. These dual narratives of loss and triumph are central to the Kremlin’s communication strategy, especially in the context of foreign policy and the war in Ukraine. Drawing on approaches from security studies, cultural semiotics, and memory studies, the article examines how fear semiosis shapes collective identity and mobilise audiences. Particular attention is given to metonymic and metaphoric strategies in conspiracy narratives promoted by political elites to reinforce cohesion and legitimise aggression. These narratives are embedded in broader cultural frameworks of strategic culture, drawing on tropes of historical grievance and enemy imagery. The study highlights how the Kremlin employs conspiracy narratives as psychological and communicative weapons to frame threats and sustain internal legitimacy.

t: Value regimes from authenticity nostalgia to xiaozi-class lifestyle: a critical assemblage analysis of treaty port commodification
abs: This paper explores commodification as a place-based dynamic of (re)assembling distributed elements and a biopolitical process of regulating subjectivity. Adopting a critical assemblage approach, I examine ongoing tourism development of “treaty port area” in China, which has shifted from heritage-themed revitalisation to xiaozi-oriented lifestyle consumption. The analysis demonstrates that (1) nostalgia assemblage and xiaozi assemblage historically emerge to commodify the treaty port; (2) the assemblages produce regimes that regulate the value of treaty port, transforming it from “historical authenticity” to “pleasure-seeking coolness” and “romantic love”; (3) these commodification processes shape consumers into distinct subject positions, respectively a local neighbourhood identity and a privileged cosmopolitan-class elitism under neoliberal-colonial logics. The paper further suggests two implications. First, commodification is not confined to signs or objects but ecologically constituted by active interactions among material, discursive, and affective elements. Second, through selective (re)organisation of semiotic resources, commodification not merely pursues free-market profits but exercises modes of governance on subjects and arranges broader political economy.

t: Music education as symbolic action: critiquing Western music education rhetoric
abs: This paper examines Western music education through Kenneth Burke's dramatism, revealing how traditional pedagogical practices function as symbolic actions perpetuating cultural hierarchies and conservative ideologies.We argue that institutionalised music education employs rhetorical mechanisms conflating scientistic and dramatistic approaches to music, particularly through repertoire selection and error correction.These mechanisms position certain works as inherently "correct" while othering alternatives, maintaining cultural supremacy that privileges Western Common Practice traditions and potentially limiting students' creative development and contemporary career opportunities.We demonstrate how institutions tacitly deploy these mechanisms, creating self-perpetuating musical conservatism that disconnects students from industrial practices and innovation.In response, we propose the Shared Music Vocabulary (SMV) as an alternative framework acknowledging music education as rhetorical symbolic action entangled with social, political, and cultural identities.This approach prioritises intellectual property generation and embraces multiple disciplines simultaneously, offering more inclusive and industrially relevant music education.

t: Emoji as interpersonal resources in LLM chatbot conversations: a social semiotic analysis of tenor and affiliation in human–AI interaction
abs: This study examines how large language model (LLM) chatbots use emoji to manage social relationships in conversations with users. Drawing on a dataset of one million chatbot–human interactions, we analyse emoji as resources for shaping interpersonal tone and building rapport. Using a social semiotic approach, we show that emoji often make chatbots appear friendly and supportive by softening requests, signalling enthusiasm, and fostering a sense of connection. However, this pattern can become formulaic, leading to overly cheerful or sycophantic responses. These interpersonal functions are analysed using the tenor system, tuning, which models how interpersonal meanings can be modified by adjusting their consequence (stakes), degree of inclusivity (scope), and the tone in which they are cast (spirit). We discuss what these findings reveal about chatbot design and the role of emoji in human–AI communication.

t: Multimodal, polysemiotic, multisemiotic: a necessary demarcation for semiotics and translation studies
abs: Very often in semiotics, but also in translation studies, a conceptual confusion is found between the terms multimodal and polysemiotic/multisemiotic. Certainly, both terms connote the presence of several semiotic systems in a cultural text, but these semiotic systems, although different (e.g. image, color, lay out, typography, graphic design), may belong to the same semiotic mode (e.g. visual). This confusion has resulted in many scholars using one term instead of the other, with the term multimodality gaining ground in their preferences. It is also certain that the occasional conceptual proposals by the French semiotic school (interaction, fusion, jonction, synergie, syncrétisme, intersemioticité, transmutation, transposition, etc.) further complicate the issue of whether a semiotic phenomenon takes place between semiotic systems or modes. This issue is of particular concern to translation scholars who argue that if translation takes place in multimodal environments, why not use the term multimodal translation instead of intersemiotic translation, transmutation, or transposition. The paper aims to present a reflection on the two terms of semiotics, multimodal and polysemiotic/multisemiotic that are also widely used in translation studies and to define their boundaries so that they can be discernible even to scholars of other research fields with which semiotics comes into contact.

t: Civil–military integration and softened authority: reconstruction of the Chinese military image in semiotic landscapes
abs: This study investigates how the Chinese military reconstructs its image through semiotic landscapes and examines how these semiotic strategies shape public perceptions of the military. Drawing on theories of discourse power, interaction ritual chains, and affective regimes of semiotic landscapes, this study constructs an integrated analytical framework and applies it to the case of the Chinese Air Force Open Day, combining walking tours, semi-structured interviews, and analysis of both offline and online semiotic representations. The findings show that the Chinese military strategically constructs rituals through semiotic means, such as the use of regional dialects, to negotiate power and elicit emotional resonance. While projecting an image of approachability and warmth to gain civilian support, these symbolic practices ultimately serve as mechanisms for legitimising official authority.

t: Constructing the prosecution-defense relationship through multimodal positioning: a corpus-based analysis of Chinese courtroom argumentation
abs: This article investigates how group value negotiation is constructed through the multimodal positioning of public prosecutors, defense lawyers, and defendants in Chinese courtroom trials. A corpus-based analysis of fifteen cases in which defendants pleaded guilty reveals that, first, public prosecutors construct themselves as appraisers for charging defendants, focusing on evidence and criminal behavior, defense lawyers act as appraisers for leniency, foregrounding defendants' confessions and personal circumstances, while defendants position themselves as lay emoters, displaying remorse. Second, both public prosecutors and defense lawyers demonstrate professionalism through modal complementarity while defendants may integrate emotional language and paralanguage to convey remorse. Third, defense lawyers and defendants engage more with judges through gaze for affiliation, although public prosecutors and defense lawyers tend to limit their gazes and use more material-mediated gestures. The findings suggest that these distinct multimodal representations are deeply intertwined with the Chinese legal-cultural context. This study provides new insights into the nature of multimodal courtroom argumentation within the civil law system.

t: “It won’t harm the hymen!” – a multimodal critical discourse analysis of the marketing discourse of tampons in China
abs: Tampons, widely used in the West, remain unfamiliar to many Chinese menstruators who mainly use pads. However, evolving gender views in China have driven tampon promotion efforts. This study examines how tampons are portrayed in promotional texts illustrated on China’s largest online shopping platform – Taobao, and how the marketing discourse of tampons reproduces, rejects, and eschews menstrual stigma maintained by Confucian gender ideologies. Adopting a feminist approach to multimodal critical discourse analysis (MCDA), I explore how once stigmatized menstrual products are now marketed as physically liberating options for menstruators in China. Data were collected from six top-seller tampon brands on Taobao. The analysis shows that tampons are marketed as a high-tech, novice-friendly solution for menstruators in China, whose premarital virginity is preserved despite the use of penetrative tampons. I argue that tampon marketing discourse in China is premised on the menstrual concealment imperative, which frames menstruators’ self-disciplinary practices as socially and physically beneficial, ultimately aligning with local gender norms.

t: Communicative action in fishermen’s coffee shops West Aceh, Indonesia
abs: This study explores the communicative dynamics in fishermen’s coffee shops in West Aceh, Indonesia. These informal spaces serve as hubs for interaction and decision-making among fishermen, whose traditions are rooted in oral and collective practices. The research examines whether these coffee shops provide an ideal speech situation an environment fostering open dialogue and free from dominance. The findings highlight significant power imbalances, with merchants dominating discussions and decision-making, often prioritizing their business interests. Laborer fishermen, constrained by dependency and physical labor, tend to accept decisions imposed by others. While these coffee shops promote social interaction and community bonding, they fail to dismantle hierarchical structures or enable egalitarian communication. This study concludes that the lifeworld and social hierarchy of fishermen in West Aceh restrict the realization of inclusive dialogue. Despite their communal role, coffee shops reflect and perpetuate existing power disparities, limiting their potential as spaces of equitable discourse.

t: Visual Citizenship. Communicating Political Opinions and Emotions on Social Media
The effectiveness of sarcastic multimodal semiotic analysis in revealing deficiencies among authority officials: a case study of Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)
abs: This study examines the role of multimodal semiotics in highlighting sarcasm embedded in the verbal and visual comments addressing the deficiencies of the Jordanian BRT project on social media platforms. Barthes’ semiotic approach was adopted to analyze 200 visual and verbal comments from Jordanians’ posts. The semiotic analysis elucidates that sarcasm is produced through a deliberate interaction of various semiotic modes combined with recontextualized socio-cultural resources. The commentators employ strategically sarcastic rhetorical techniques to articulate societal discontent with corruption, lack of accountability, and disillusionment with authoritative figures. These sarcastic techniques encompass comparisons, personification, rhetorical questions, proverbs, intertextuality, and exaggeration. The employment of sarcasm has critically interrogated the corrupt discourse of authority figures, shedding light on the intricate power dynamics and inherent inefficiencies and nuances that permeate their discourse. This analytical lens situates these figures as an out-group, susceptible to ridicule by the in-group community that bears the adverse consequences of corruption. It is anticipated that this investigation will yield significant contributions to subsequent research, providing valuable insights into multimodal semiotic analysis.

t: Discursive construction of legitimation and delegitimation: a comparative critical discourse analysis of a public debate over Singapore’s capital punishment
abs: This article investigates how Singapore's capital punishment is legitimised and delegitimised in public discourse, focusing on the written exchanges between Sir Richard Branson and Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs from October 2022 to April 2023. Drawing on the theoretical perspectives of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) and Van Leeuwen's legitimation framework, the study uncovers distinct patterns in how MHA and Branson legitimise and delegitimise the contentious social practice of capital punishment in Singapore, respectively. The analysis details the discursive and linguistic realisations of these legitimation and delegitimation constructions and demonstrates how analyses of representations of social practices can be integrated with legitimation and delegitimation analyses. Additionally, the article's comparative analysis sheds light on the ways legitimation and delegitimation discourses can be shaped by international human-rights advocacy and national policy interests to influence public opinion on contentious social practices such as capital punishment.

t: “Waste-sorting is the new fashion”: waste, power, and the semiotic landscape
abs: This study examines how the Chinese government uses multiple semiotic resources, in both online and offline contexts, to (re)shape citizens' behaviors and construct knowledge about wastesorting under the recent national waste-sorting policy. Informed by Foucault's notion of governmentality, we show how governmental strategies operate at the level of both material artifacts (e.g. rubbish bins in one city) as well as in national media reports (i.e. news articles from state-sponsored news websites). By integrating geosemiotics with multimodal critical discourse analysis, we demonstrate how rubbish bins visually, interactively, and spatially construct wastesorting as “fashionable” public behavior. At the same time, online news media reports complement these artifacts by highlighting certain elements of the new bins (e.g. CCTV cameras and card-swiping systems) and by capturing strategic moments of residents using the bins, thus supporting and promoting actions that are aligned with national policy.

t: Multimodal representation and ideological framing of social actors in Kenya’s anti-police brutality Twitter activism
abs: This study examines how multimodal resources in Kenyan Twitter activism against police brutality construct representations of social actors and conveys ideological positions. Drawing on 496 purposively sampled tweets under the #JusticeForKianjokomaBrothers, the study employs a multimodal critical discourse analysis approach. It examines how semiotic resources frame victims, state actors, activists, and family while exposing embedded ideologies. Linguistic resources such as naming and familial nouns, humanize victims as innocent and vulnerable, reinforced by emotive visual cues. In contrast, police are delegitimized through collectivized nouns, negative lexical items and symbolic imagery. Activists are portrayed as a unified collective using plural nouns and solidarity symbols, while maternal grief and collective suffering frame the family emphasizing the social impact. The findings present police brutality as systemic, stress the moral obligation to resist and position digital activism as a powerful tool for social change. This research contributes to digital protest discourse by showing how multimodal elements mobilize public sentiment and challenge entrenched power structures.

t: Multimodality of the non-leading teacher in collaborative teaching
abs: This study examines multimodality in bilingual co-teaching, focusing on the embodied conduct of the “non-leading” teacher. Drawing on multimodal conversation analysis, it investigates how co-teachers use verbal and nonverbal conduct to coordinate instructional tasks. The analysis demonstrates that even nonvocal actions, such as gestures and body movements, play a vital role in achieving collaborative teaching objectives. By observing EFL classroom interactions in Korea, the study highlights the non-leading teacher's active participation through gesture alignment, premonitory actions, and supplementary embodiment. These findings reveal the simultaneous and layered nature of teacher collaboration, challenging conventional notions that treat nonvocal behavior as secondary to verbal interaction. The research contributes to co-teaching literature by offering a multimodal perspective on teacher collaboration, emphasizing the interplay of verbal and embodied actions. It also provides a framework for evaluating co-teaching partnerships based on observable multimodal behaviors, offering practical implications for teacher training and assessment.

t: What AI knows about breast cancer: an exploratory visual discourse analysis on AI-generated breast cancer advertisement images
abs: This study conducted an exploratory visual discourse analysis aiming to investigate how AI-generated breast cancer advertisement images understand and speak to the public about breast cancer. We found that breast cancer advertising culture and social biases toward breast cancer together profoundly influence the visual interpretation of breast cancer in AI-generated breast cancer advertising images. Specifically, we identified four dominant discourses (You should enjoy breast cancer; You should fear breast cancer; Pink is breast cancer; You can't face it), three dissenting discourses (The calm elderly breast cancer patients; The association of breast cancer with women's nurturing function; The mutually supportive and friendly female social supporters) and two invisible discourses (Medical information about breast cancer; The absence of male figures). This study suggests the need to avoid a homogeneous and generalized understanding of AI image generation algorithms and provides suggestions for brands to review AI-generated images of breast cancer advertisements.

t: Revolutionary things: the making of South Korea’s Candlelight Protests
abs: This study examines the making of South Korea’s Candlelight Protests from a material perspective to comprehend citizens’ experiences and aesthetics, using an integrated conceptual framework that combines interdisciplinary discourse through Peircean triadic semiotics based on possibility, actuality, and rationality. I describe the theoretical background of a new trend in materiality studies as well as contemporary citizenship based on the concept of making. I then present a multidimensional diagram of the conceptual framework, followed by a brief timeline of the Candlelight Protests, focusing on the key moments and material artifacts that affected weekly civic participation. I performed a material cultural analysis of protest-making along two main axes of materiality and summarized the findings in an extended diagram: experiences, which concentrates on protest objects and events, including candlelight, protest signs, and Internet memes; and aesthetics, which emphasizes their assembled relations and the power of subjectivity in the relevant historical and cultural milieu of Gwanghwamun Square.

t: The language of reality: a semiotic guide for shaping thought about American education
abs: Almost everyone in the United States experiences some form of schooling and thus forms opinions of what schools are, falls victim to folk theory about curriculum, and lives their lives by the myths about American education. Truth and reality have become debatable concepts in public language. The semiological concept of myth plays an influential role in these debates. However, just as myths can be used to confuse and convince, if remythified they also can be used to clarify and conjure up a new language of reality. In this article, I critique the myth of Critical Race Theory (CRT) in US schools. I then extend the work of Barthes ([1957] 1972. Mythologies. Translated by Annette Lavers. New York: Hill and Wang) in applying a third semiological chain that acts to remythify this myth with a new, more positive meaning and reality, with hopes that this process could be extended to other American education mythologies.

t: Framing insecurity: the ideological functions of discourse markers in select Nigerian political interviews
abs: What ideological functions do discourse markers (DMs) perform? Previous research on DMs has largely been descriptive and paid little attention on their broad socio-cultural and ideological roles. This study aims to fill that gap by maximising the insights of critical discourse analysis (CDA) to examine DMs utilised by Presidential Media Advisers (PMAs) in political interviews on insecurity in Nigeria. 366 DMs are identified and categorised into structural (43.2%), referential (28.4%), interpersonal (19.9%), and cognitive (8.5%) types. Findings reveal that PMAs strategically deploy DMs to achieve various higher-order ideological aims: legitimising the government’s inaction (e.g. “you know,” “yes,” “just”), recontextualising insecurity and governmental responses (e.g. “because,” “but,” “and,” “or”), and diverting attention from critical issues (e.g. “now,” “so,” “well”). The study highlights the significant role DMs play in shaping political discourse and public perception of national security in Nigeria.

t: A study of Pinyin as social practice in China’s commercial linguistic landscape
abs: Despite its status as an auxiliary notational system and a pedagogical aid for Chinese learning in China’s language policy and planning, the use and classification of Pinyin in China’s linguistic landscape has caused much confusion for researchers. Through an investigation of the use of Pinyin in the commercial linguistic landscape of Quanzhou, a second-tier coastal city of China, this study finds that Pinyin is used in various ways and associated with different brand positionings. Despite various ways of using Pinyin and different brand positionings, the appropriation of Pinyin points to the commodification of languages and scripts in modern societies. The use of Pinyin contributes to distinctive cosmopolitanism which values the visual salience rather than the referential function of languages and scripts.

t: Muddying the waters on climate change: conflicting positions articulated in Instagram posts about Greta Thunberg’s 2023 arrest
abs: Climate change is an existential threat. Despite facts that suggest otherwise, climate scepticism remains salient especially on social media. Online information and entertainment increasingly shape our attitudes and behaviours, with fake-news and polarisation being commonplace. In this paper, we examine what discourses are articulated on social media posts about climate change. Using multimodal critical discourse studies, we analyse how images, lexica and video in a sample of Instagram posts about Greta Thunberg articulate a variety of viewpoints. Despite some hopeful findings, a number of posts serve to promote climate sceptic views, a trend that has the potential to further the interests of the fossil fuel industry. We find posts are highly polarised, disregard meaningful dialogue and consideration of facts based on a scientific consensus on the causes and consequences of climate change. Instead, posts muddy the waters in advancing knowledge on how to promote climate action.

t: How defendants frame remorse: a pragmatic and transitivity analysis of allocution statements in Chinese and American courts
abs: Defendants’ allocution statements, formal declarations made during sentencing, provide an opportunity for defendants to speak in court, express remorse, deliver apologies, and request leniency. Therefore, examining the sincerity of their apologies and the successful expression of remorse becomes crucial as these factors may impact their chances of receiving a lower sentence. Three cases are investigated in this study: one in America (with three allocution statements) and two in China (with two allocution statements). These cases were selected to explore how allocution statements function within two distinct legal and cultural contexts, despite differences in courtroom procedures. Adopting an approach that combines pragmatics and functional linguistics, with a focus on the apology speech act and transitivity patterns, the study attempts to establish an analytical framework based on the collected data and discourse analysis. By analysing five allocution statements, this study demonstrates how defendants utilize various allocution categories, subcategories, and transitivity processes to either effectively convey or inadequately express remorse. Each pragmatic and linguistic choice contributes to the perceived authenticity of their statements, potentially affecting sentencing results.

t: Forensic analysis of populist discourse and multimodal craft of consensus in Netanyahu's July 2024 Congressional address
abs: This study employs Natural Language Processing and semio-discursive tools to analyze the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Congressional speech on July 2024, within the context of populist communication. The research work examines the multimodal – linguistic, auditory, and visual – elements of Netanyahu's speech to uncover the underlying rhetorical and communicative techniques. Grounded in the conceptualization of populism as an ideational/communicative phenomenon, the study investigates the key radical right-wing populist frames and strategies Netanyahu incorporates in his address and how these frames and strategies interact with media dynamics and citizen engagement, particularly in a hybrid media environment characterized by a convergence of mass and interpersonal communication. The findings aim to advance Forensic Linguistics by demonstrating the potential of a mixed-methods research design in dissecting complex political rhetoric, offering valuable insights for scholars, media analysts, and GenAI researchers interested in the interplay of technology, media, and populist communication.

t: Political othering and polarisation in Nigeria’s online electoral discourse: towards a culture of inter-political party tolerance
abs: During elections in Nigeria, views expressed by supporters of political parties tend to exclude others and frame members of opposing parties as inferior. This paper examines othering and polarisation related to political party affiliations by analysing 9,816 Facebook comments focused on Nigeria’s 2023 general elections using critical discourse analysis. The findings reveal that polarisation and othering of outgroup political parties and their supporters occur through two discursive strategies: the psychiatrisation of political support and the attribution of otherness through electoral clientelism. The study concludes by proposing a culture of inter-political party tolerance that incorporates indigenous knowledge systems to mitigate othering. This research adds to the growing body of literature on othering and affective polarisation between groups, particularly in the African context.

t: An examination of delegitimation in the activist discourse of Ghana's #FixTheCountry lead convener Oliver Barker-Vormawor
abs: This article examines the delegitimation strategies used by Oliver Barker-Vormawor, political activist and the lead convener of Ghana’s #FixTheCountry movement. The analysis of Barker-Vormawor’s Facebook posts reveals that he employed three main delegitimation strategies to formulate a conviction rhetoric aimed at discrediting Ghana’s governance under the presidency of Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo and validating his activism and the goals of his #FixTheCountry movement. These strategies are authorization, rationalization, and moral evaluation and they help Barker-Vormawor to construct himself as a patriot, a noble revolutionary, and a selfless leader who has the welfare of the Ghanaian people at heart. The study extends research on the construction of online activist discourses and demonstrates that research on the (de)legitimation mechanisms of “unconstitutional authorities” is necessary to enhance our understanding of (online) activist discourse and how contentious politics is conceptualized and performed.

t: Erotic capital in digital age: a multimodal analysis of the idolization of fresh meat elite on Xiaohongshu
abs: This paper examines the digital cultural phenomenon termed “fresh meat elite” shaped by socio-economic and cultural influences in contemporary China, focusing on TikTok CEO Shouzi Chew. A multimodal critical discourse analysis applied on the digital narratives from Xiaohongshu reveals how young Chinese women construct and consume this desirable male image, subtly infusing it with economic, cultural and erotic capital, resonating with dominant neoliberal norms. Our examination extends to Chew’s spouse, labeled as a “high-quality woman,” foregrounding the interplay between masculine fascination and females’ evolving self-positions. The discourse on Xiaohongshu significantly fuels the “fresh meat elite” typology’s consumerist aspect, which hybridizes Western, Pan-East Asian masculine paradigms. Our findings reveal an empowering edge to this behavior, asserting the female agency in delineating their preferred masculinity. However, the research flags potential boomerang effects, arguing that these narratives might ingeniously embed neoliberal, post-feminist ideologies, reinstating traditional societal norms around personal accomplishments, body aesthetics, and gender binaries. This paper underscores the critical need for a nuanced comprehension of shifting gender roles amidst the intersectionality of consumerism, digital culture, and the contemporary Chinese socio-cultural matrix.

t: From monologues to multimodal perspectivization: strategies for affective commercialization via Boys Love (BL) manga covers
abs: This article examines how affect is multimodally configured on manga covers in Japan. Focusing on commercial Boys Love (BL) manga, a genre where affect is central to female readers’ engagement with homoerotic stories featuring male characters, the covers become crucial for producers to strategize in engaging their audience. Using Martin & White’s Affect framework and the concept of “focalization,” the monologue titles on fifty BL manga covers and their interaction with character visuals are analyzed. The strategic use of three types of monologues reveals patterns of affect that align with various appeal points for BL readers, demonstrating how titles are not just representational but also fulfill an interactional function. Additionally, titles and visuals work together to focalize different perspectives of the same affect, enhancing emotional resonance of the covers through multimodal perspectivization. This study highlights semiotic strategies that maximize the minimal affordance and space to circulate affect for affective commercialization of media within Japan’s highly commercialized popular culture landscape.

t: Embracing transgression(s) : a critical-dialogical semiotic approach on how “rhetorical plasticity” shapes contemporary far-right ideological reproduction
abs: The seemingly trivial embrace between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Argentine President Javier Milei at the 2024 G7 summit exemplifies a significant rhetorical mechanism in far-right strategies. This semiotic gesture creates a transgressive political space where rhetorical plasticity operates, enabling leaders to reconcile conflicting ideologies and adapt messages across contexts. This dynamic raises concerns about fluid ideological boundaries, potentially undermining democratic foundations. By examining the argumentative-linguistic structures in such interactions, we see how language encodes and reproduces far-right ideologies while masking the absence of a coherent ideological project. “Plasticity” thus constructs a heterogeneous framework providing superficial consistency, allowing leaders to exploit fleeting opportunities. Rather than seeking a dialogic balance between political actors and interpreters, this approach highlights the inherent ethical bonds linking speakers to their enunciations. Recognizing that meaning and responsibility derive from enunciation itself – rather than “true intentions” – provides insights into how far-right movements use symbolic acts to legitimize their rise and disseminate ideologies across diverse socio-political landscapes.

t: Semiotics and framing of Ukrainian refugees in Spanish political discourse: a linguistic and cognitive analysis
abs: This study analyzes how four major Spanish political parties use semiotic resources on Twitter to portray Ukrainian refugees, employing corpus linguistics and cognitive framing. Drawing on Saussure’s semiology, Van Dijk’s discourse theory, Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis, and Lakoff’s framing theory, we examine how words function as signs that frame ideological positions. Partido Popular (PP) emphasizes individual liberty and national identity, PSOE highlights diplomacy and humanitarianism, Unidas Podemos (UP) assigns blame to specific countries while showing solidarity with Ukraine, and VOX advocates strict refugee policies with an anti-communist stance. This detailed linguistic and semiotic analysis reveals how the parties’ language choices, informed by cognitive and semiotic frames, reflect underlying power structures and ideological biases, offering important insights into the dynamics of political discourse around refugees, and how language shapes public perception.

t: Lessons in influence: unveiling the multimodal identity construction of female teacher influencers on Xiaohongshu
abs: This study investigates the multimodal identity construction of female teacher influencers on Xiaohongshu, China’s leading female-centric social media platform. Utilizing a robust theoretical framework grounded in social semiotics and Multimodal Critical Discourse Analysis (MCDA), we analyzed 51 representative posts from 16 prominent influencers. Our analysis reveals that female teacher influencers celebrate a form of female empowerment deeply intertwined with consumerist values. Their social media narratives intricately blend professional identity with consumerist desire, employing professional symbols such as educational background and office settings to establish credibility, while positioning themselves within a neoliberal framework that emphasizes success through consumption and aesthetic presentation. Our findings highlight a marked shift towards a commodified form of empowerment among female intellectuals in digital media, showcasing the limitations and contradictions inherent in these representations. This research contributes to the scholarly discourse on gender, professionalism, and digital media, and prompts critical reflection on how neoliberal ideologies shape contemporary notions of female success and attractiveness. Future research should explore the longitudinal impact of these consumerist narratives on both influencers and their audiences and investigate whether these patterns of empowerment are universally applicable or culturally specific.

t: Graffiti and Urban transformation: the ideological discourse in the semiotic landscape of the Asturian Mining Valley
abs: In language contact situations, linguistic landscapes are places where minority languages fight for visibility and survival. This study focuses on Asturies, a region of Spain where Spanish is the hegemonic language, while Asturian, a minoritized language, confronts numerous obstacles in administrative and educational contexts. This research examines graffiti in the Asturian Mining Valley, an area undergoing urban revitalization after the decline of the mining industry. By adopting a qualitative approach, the goal is to analyze how symbols, written discourse, and spatial arrangements in graffiti are used to build meaning and display identities, ideologies, and power relations related to the Mining Valley’s urban transformation. Results show diverse frames of meaning tied to identity negotiation, representation, and socio-political identities within the region’s linguistic landscape. Those include responses to mining reconversion, workers’ rights, anti-fascism, global movements, and feminist advocacy. This research enhances the understanding of linguistic landscapes in communities experiencing ideological conflict and social change.

t: A comparative critical analysis of official and personal social media videos on being and becoming old in China
abs: This study delves into ageing as it is depicted through social media videos in China. Through a critical analysis of 40 short-form videos, it compares how older people are discursively constructed by official agents and individual content creators to uncover their underlying ideological interests. Findings show that official videos tend to portray older people as socially disconnected and lonely whereas personal videos tend to showcase the jovial and inspirational aspects of growing old. They also reveal that official videos are exclusively situated in urban settings while personal videos also depict older people in rural and relatively modest settings. These findings reflect and reinforce the pathologisation and othering of older people and reveal ideologies linked to communitarianism and governmentality and the commodification of old age in the Chinese socio-political and socio-cultural ecosystem.

t: Teachers’ gestures in synchronous online language classrooms: embodied elicitation strategies for student participation
abs: Classroom interaction research has increasingly embraced the analysis of multimodal resources, including teacher gestures, alongside verbal input in eliciting student contributions. This focus has extended to online video-mediated classrooms, where such strategies remain equally indispensable. Employing a multimodal Conversation Analysis approach, this study examines an English language teacher’s multimodal interactional strategy to elicit student contributions in online video-mediated interactions. Drawing on screen recordings of online English language classrooms in higher education, the analysis reveals how the teacher established embodied elicitation strategies as an online classroom norm to facilitate and balance multiparty student participation through hand gestures, empowering students to regulate their involvement through their gestures. This study provides deeper insights into the role of teacher gestures in online classroom interactions, shedding light on how the affordances and constraints of different interactional environments shape their use. The findings offer valuable implications for enhancing the pedagogical practices of both pre-service and in-service teachers.

t: A boon or a bane: multimodal figurative framing in Chinese and foreign BRI-themed cartoons
abs: The present research aims to marry insights from Cognitive Linguistics to those of Communication Studies and propose an integrated framework known as multimodal figurative framing. Two comparable multimodal corpora, consisting of BRI-themed cartoons retrieved from China Daily (CD: 152 cartoons) and Google News & Images (GN&I: 56 cartoons), are compiled and examined to explore the theoretical and practical values of multimodal figurative devices in framing abstract political topics. Through an integration of quantitative and qualitative analysis, the study reveals that the employment of different figurative frames in these cartoons leads to contrasting interpretations of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). In the CD corpus, a total of 15 multimodal metonymies and 13 metaphors can be identified, which serve to frame BRI as a beneficial endeavour associated with equality, win-win cooperation, peaceful progress, shared prosperity, multilateral inclusiveness, and green sustainability. In contrast, the GN&I corpus employs 9 multimodal metonymies and 11 metaphors to frame BRI as a detrimental scheme characterised by attributes such as destruction, aggression, deception, hegemony, competition, contradiction, and invasion. The study helps lay bare opposite attitudes toward the BRI, which stem from divergent political ideologies.
